implementation_notes: The classic realization on POSIX systems: pthread_key_create() allocates one process-wide key (optionally with a destructor that runs at thread exit), pthread_setspecific() and pthread_getspecific() bind and read a void* in the calling thread's thread-specific data area, and a small accessor function is the TS Object Proxy that hides the key. The key is allocated once per process (guard it with pthread_once()), while each thread creates its own object lazily on first access. Use the key-based form when the per-thread object is created at runtime, when one type needs several independent per-thread slots, or when dynamically allocated per-thread resources must be freed by a destructor; the C11 storage-class form below is simpler for plain per-thread variables but has no destructor and no runtime slots.
pitfalls: Using a key before pthread_key_create() has run - or after pthread_key_delete() - is undefined behaviour; the standard rejected making key creation idempotent, so wrap it in pthread_once().
A destructor that re-associates a value with its key makes the implementation repeat destruction, up to PTHREAD_DESTRUCTOR_ITERATIONS; a destructor that always re-sets the key can leak or loop.
There is a fixed per-process key budget (PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX; pthread_key_create() fails with EAGAIN), so keys must be allocated once, not per request or per thread.

variants.name: C11 _Thread_local storage duration (thread_local in C23)
variants.implementation_notes: C11 added a storage-class specifier: _Thread_local (spelled thread_local in C23) declares an object with thread storage duration, so the name refers to a distinct object in every thread and no key, collection or accessor is needed. It applies to file-scope objects, to block-scope declarations combined with static or extern, and it must appear on every declaration of the same object; unlike pthreads keys it cannot hold a runtime-created per-object slot and it offers no destructor hook, so it suits plain per-thread values, counters, buffers with static storage, and pointers whose cleanup is handled elsewhere. GCC and Clang offer the older __thread extension (C99-era) with similar portability caveats.
variants.code_sketch:
#include <threads.h>

static _Thread_local struct ctx ctx_cur;   /* one object per thread */

struct ctx *ctx(void) { return &ctx_cur; } /* no key, no lookup, no destructor */

void bump(void) { ++ctx_cur.count; }        /* still a plain variable access */
pitfalls: _Thread_local cannot express a per-thread slot created at runtime and cannot run cleanup: any malloc'd per-thread data still needs a pthread key destructor (or tss_t from C11 threads.h) to be freed.
__thread is a compiler extension, not ISO C; code that must compile as C99 with pedantic diagnostics cannot rely on it, and the two spellings cannot be mixed across a declaration.
A pointer stored in a thread-local object must not escape to another thread: the pointee is not protected by the storage duration, and the object itself disappears when its thread exits.
